cluster_genes.affinage_functional_annotation: BRPF1 is a multivalent chromatin reader and scaffold that recruits and activates the MOZ/KAT6A, MORF/KAT6B, and HBO1/KAT7 lysine acetyltransferase complexes, thereby catalyzing histone H3K23 acetylation and propionylation essential for gene regulation in hematopoietic stem cells, neural progenitors, and embryonic stem cells [PMID:26626149, PMID:27500495, PMID:32010779, PMID:36711238]. Its PWWP domain reads H3K36me3 [PMID:20400950], its PZP (PHD–zinc-knuckle–PHD) domain bivalently engages the histone H3 tail and nucleosomal DNA to promote DNA unwrapping and chromatin accessibility [PMID:26626149, PMID:31711755], and its bromodomain recognizes mono- and di-acetyllysine marks on histones H2A, H3, and H4 as well as non-histone partners such as ILF3 [PMID:24333487, PMID:25281266, PMID:33554132, PMID:38072045]. Loss-of-function BRPF1 variants abolish H3K23 acylation and cause syndromic intellectual disability in humans, while conditional knockout in mice produces embryonic lethality, bone marrow failure, and severe neurodevelopmental defects including reduced dendritic complexity and impaired synaptic transmission [PMID:27939640, PMID:27939639, PMID:25568313, PMID:27500495, PMID:31213987].

H2AC7 encodes histone H2A type 1-D, a replication-dependent core histone that is among the most abundant H2A variants in human cells and is organized within the major HIST1 gene cluster on chromosome 6p21-p22 [PMID:12408966, PMID:9439656]. The protein is alpha-N-acetylated at its N-terminus and carries acetylation at Lys-5 or phosphorylation at Ser-1 as its principal post-translational modifications [PMID:16457589, PMID:16319397]. H2AC7 localizes to the nucleus as a component of stable nucleosomal complexes and is also present in purified human sperm chromatin, consistent with a role in packaging paternal DNA transmitted at fertilization [PMID:35271311, PMID:21630459].

KAT2A (GCN5) is a versatile lysine acyltransferase that serves as the catalytic subunit of the SAGA and ATAC coactivator complexes, integrating metabolic acyl-CoA pools with chromatin-based gene regulation in development, immunity, and cancer. Within these complexes, the Ada2 subunit allosterically enhances KAT2A activity by promoting acetyl-CoA binding [PMID:30224453], and KAT2A acetylates histone H3 primarily at K9 and K14—with its bromodomain reading H3K14ac to license subsequent H3K18ac—as well as histone variant H2A.Z.1 [PMID:25106422, PMID:31527837]. Beyond acetylation, KAT2A functions as a succinyltransferase (H3K79 succinylation via nuclear α-KGDH-supplied succinyl-CoA, controlled by active-site residue Y645) and as a lactyltransferase (histone H3 lactylation using lactyl-CoA generated by nuclear ACSS2), and it acylates non-histone substrates including TFEB, α-tubulin, EGR2, VCP, PKM2, and influenza NP [PMID:29211711, PMID:39561764, PMID:31750630, PMID:31878840, PMID:28723564, PMID:38145956]. KAT2A is essential for mouse embryogenesis—loss causes dorsal mesoderm failure and extensive apoptosis—and in the immune system it is required for IL-2-driven T cell responses and iNKT cell development; its stability is regulated by autophagy through a conserved LIR domain [PMID:11017084, PMID:28424240, PMID:31878840].

KAT6A (MOZ/MYST3) is a MYST-family lysine acetyltransferase that functions as the catalytic subunit of a tetrameric complex with BRPF1/2/3, ING5, and EAF6 to acetylate histone H3 (at K9, K14, and K23) and non-histone substrates including p53, SMAD3, and COP1, thereby regulating transcription of developmental genes, hematopoietic stem cell maintenance programs, and senescence pathways [PMID:18794358, PMID:16702405, PMID:25772242, PMID:33995658]. KAT6A is recruited to unmethylated CpG island-containing promoters via N-terminal winged helix domains that bind CpG-rich DNA and nucleosomal dyad sequences, and to acetylated chromatin via tandem PHD fingers that recognize H3K14ac, establishing a feed-forward loop for H3K9/K23 acetylation at target loci such as HOXA9, Meis1, and Tbx1 [PMID:36537216, PMID:36754959, PMID:22713874, PMID:22921202]. KAT6A-deposited H3K9ac is read by the YEATS-domain protein ENL to promote transcriptional elongation in AML, and oncogenic fusions (MOZ-TIF2, MOZ-CBP) drive leukemogenesis by aberrantly recruiting CBP/p300 to CpG-rich developmental gene promoters and conferring self-renewal to committed progenitors [PMID:34853079, PMID:12676584, PMID:15607963, PMID:32997997]. KAT6A suppresses cellular senescence by maintaining H3K9ac and H3K27ac at loci encoding INK4A-ARF pathway inhibitors, and its loss in the nervous system impairs synaptic plasticity and Wnt signaling through transcriptional downregulation of Rspo2 [PMID:25772242, PMID:24307508, PMID:38758792].

TADA2A is a transcriptional adaptor protein that serves as a core scaffolding subunit of the PCAF, STAGA, and ATAC histone acetyltransferase complexes, where it bridges acidic activation domains of transcription factors (VP16, GCN4) with TBP and potentiates GCN5/PCAF-mediated histone acetylation [PMID:1638630, PMID:7642611, PMID:9674425, PMID:18838386]. Within the catalytic HAT module formed by Ada2/Ada3/Gcn5, TADA2A activates the intrinsically weak acetyltransferase activity of GCN5 through its SANT domain, which enhances acetyl-CoA co-substrate binding rather than histone substrate recognition [PMID:30224453, PMID:11773077]. TADA2A-containing complexes (ATAC) preferentially direct histone H4 K5/K12 acetylation, distinguishing them from the paralogous TADA2B-containing SAGA-type complexes that target H3 K9/K14, and this Ada2-dependent acetylation is required for the transition from transcription initiation to elongation [PMID:17030603, PMID:28115623]. Polyglutamine-expanded ataxin-7 incorporated into TADA2A-containing STAGA dominantly inhibits nucleosomal histone acetylation, linking TADA2A complex dysfunction to spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 [PMID:15932940].

YEATS2 is a chromatin reader subunit of the ATAC histone acetyltransferase complex that recognizes acetylated and crotonylated histone H3 (H3K27ac, H3K27cr) via its YEATS domain to sustain promoter-proximal histone acetylation and activate transcription of growth, metabolic, and DNA repair genes across multiple cancer contexts [PMID:29057918, PMID:39349460, PMID:40810390]. YEATS2 recruits acetyltransferases including GCN5/KAT2A, KAT5, and p300 to target promoters, maintaining H3K9ac, H3K14ac, and H3K27cr marks that drive expression of oncogenic programs such as MYC, TGFBR2, RAD50, ETS1, and ribosomal genes [PMID:41776086, PMID:41708952, PMID:40040791, PMID:29057918]. Its chromatin engagement is positively regulated by O-GlcNAcylation at Thr604, which strengthens ATAC complex assembly, and by TNF-α-induced tyrosine dephosphorylation of the YEATS domain, which enhances enhancer RNA binding [PMID:40541806, PMID:40216980]. Beyond chromatin reading, YEATS2 physically interacts with TAK1 to sustain NF-κB signaling in pancreatic and hepatocellular carcinoma, and in Drosophila neurons it governs dopaminergic gene expression and calcium homeostasis [PMID:34686948, PMID:41962409, PMID:38128822].

ZZZ3 is a dedicated nuclear subunit of the ATAC histone acetyltransferase complex, a ~700 kDa assembly biochemically distinct from SAGA that harbors dual HAT activities (GCN5/KAT2 and ATAC2/KAT14) and stimulates nucleosome remodeling by ISWI and SWI/SNF-family complexes [PMID:16428443, PMID:18327268]. Its ZZ-type zinc finger domain directly recognizes the N-terminal alanine of histone H3 through an acidic cavity, thereby recruiting the ATAC complex to chromatin to promote H3K9 acetylation at promoters and activate target gene expression [PMID:30217978]. O-GlcNAcylation of the ATAC subunit YEATS2 strengthens ZZZ3–YEATS2 interaction on chromatin, stabilizing ATAC complex occupancy and sustaining H3K9 acetylation [PMID:40541806]. ZZZ3 also engages oncogenic fusion transcription factors (TAZ-CAMTA1, YAP-TFE3) and super-enhancer elements to drive context-specific transcriptional programs, and is required for ribosome biogenesis, mTOR signaling, and proliferation in human embryonic stem cells [PMID:33913810, PMID:39376717, PMID:38701777].

CARS2 is the mitochondrial cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase that performs two essential and coupled catalytic functions: it aminoacylates mitochondrial tRNA(Cys) to support mitochondrial translation and oxidative phosphorylation complex assembly, and it acts as the principal cysteine persulfide synthase (CPERS), generating reactive sulfur species (CysSSH, polysulfides) that regulate mitochondrial biogenesis, bioenergetics, and diverse cell-type-specific processes [PMID:29079736, PMID:25787132]. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in CARS2 cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency and epileptic encephalopathy, and Cars2 knockout is embryonically lethal in mice [PMID:25361775, PMID:25787132, PMID:32012740]. CARS2-derived supersulfides exert anti-inflammatory effects in macrophages through IL-10/STAT3 signaling, restrain CD4+ T cell proliferation to maintain intestinal immune homeostasis, drive brown adipogenesis via persulfidation of EBF2 enhancing its interaction with PPARγ and BRG1, and protect against excitotoxic neuronal death by scavenging reactive oxygen species [PMID:35381443, PMID:40303402, PMID:41849685, PMID:41506554]. Impairment of CARS2 persulfide production in knock-in mice compromises fracture healing and accelerates osteoarthritis, and in hematopoietic progenitors it suppresses erythroid commitment by reducing mitochondrial function [PMID:39983344, PMID:41270746].

MGA is a dual-specificity transcription factor that heterodimerizes with MAX and employs both a bHLH-leucine zipper (bHLHZip) domain for E-box binding and a T-box domain for T-box element binding, functioning primarily as a transcriptional repressor and scaffolding subunit of the non-canonical Polycomb repressive complex PRC1.6 (with PCGF6, E2F6, L3MBTL2, and RING1A/B) [PMID:10601024, PMID:22325352, PMID:29381691]. CRISPR ablation of MGA eliminates PRC1.6 genomic occupancy and de-represses MYC/E2F target genes, meiosis-related genes, and endodermal fate determinants (GATA4/6, SOX17), establishing MGA as an essential scaffold that recruits PRC1.6 to specific promoters and additionally recruits the SETDB1/ATF7IP complex to deposit H3K9me3 at meiosis-related loci [PMID:29381691, PMID:33523934, PMID:40727931]. MGA acts as a tumor suppressor whose loss accelerates lung adenocarcinoma progression, drives CLL-to-Richter's transformation via the MGA–NME1–OXPHOS axis, and cooperates with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 in AML, while in development it is essential for pluripotent cell survival through polyamine synthesis regulation and for dorsoventral patterning via a MGA–MAX–SMAD4 complex that activates BMP signaling [PMID:34236315, PMID:39083585, PMID:38454121, PMID:25516968, PMID:24525188]. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in MGA cause premature ovarian insufficiency in humans and subfertility in mice [PMID:39545409].

NAA50 is a ribosome-associated N-terminal acetyltransferase (NatE catalytic subunit) that co-translationally acetylates the α-amino group of initiator methionine-retaining protein N-termini, with preference for Met-Leu, Met-Met, and other Met-Xaa sequences, and competes kinetically with methionine aminopeptidases to determine initiator methionine retention [PMID:25886145, PMID:27484799]. Its GNAT-fold active site contains a methionine-specific pocket anchored by conserved histidine and tyrosine catalytic residues, and it physically associates with both subunits of the NatA complex (Naa10/Naa15) through evolutionarily conserved contacts that promote catalytic crosstalk [PMID:21900231, PMID:31155310]. In addition to possessing Nα-acetyltransferase activity, NAA50 exhibits Nε-lysine acetyltransferase and autoacetylation activities that modulate its substrate specificity in vitro [PMID:19744929]. In metazoans, NAA50 is essential for sister-chromatid cohesion: it N-terminally acetylates the cohesin subunit Scc1, supports the cohesin–sororin interaction, and functions antagonistically to NatA in cohesion regulation [PMID:14653991, PMID:27422821, PMID:27996020].

OGA (MGEA5) is the primary cytoplasmic and nuclear β-N-acetylglucosaminidase that removes O-GlcNAc from serine/threonine residues of intracellular proteins, functioning as the sole eraser opposing the O-GlcNAc transferase OGT in a tightly counter-regulated signaling cycle [PMID:11341771, PMID:37907462]. Substrate recognition extends beyond the catalytic active-site pocket: a conserved peptide-binding groove in the stalk domain confers substrate selectivity, and cancer-associated stalk mutations rewire substrate preference toward proline-containing motifs, altering downstream p53 stability and cell motility [PMID:20863279, PMID:38838015]. The C-terminal pseudo-HAT domain forms catalytically incompetent homodimers that allosterically regulate the active site, and cryo-EM structures of the OGT–OGA complex show that OGT disrupts OGA dimerization while OGA occupies OGT's substrate groove, establishing a mutual-inhibition mechanism that limits futile O-GlcNAc cycling [PMID:37907462, PMID:16356930]. OGA is itself post-translationally regulated through ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation mediated by the E3 ligases UBR5 and TRIM33/RBM14, and it participates in DNA repair by deglycosylating NONO and Ku70/80 to facilitate non-homologous end joining [PMID:38755129, PMID:38678556, PMID:34135314].

PSME3 (PA28γ/REGγ) is a nuclear 11S proteasome activator that promotes ubiquitin-independent degradation of diverse substrates through the 20S proteasome, thereby controlling cell cycle progression, innate immune signaling, stem cell pluripotency, and antigen presentation. Substrate recognition employs distinct mechanisms: phosphorylation-dependent binding for MAFA [PMID:21646385], O-GlcNAcylation of PSME3 Ser111 for Ddx6 degradation in embryonic stem cells [PMID:34260942], and mutual SUMO–SIM interactions for CP2c degradation during cell cycle transit [PMID:36706181]. Beyond proteasome activation, PSME3 functions as a molecular scaffold that bridges MDM2 and p53 to facilitate p53 ubiquitination and degradation, limiting apoptosis after DNA damage [PMID:18309296]. In innate immunity, PSME3 degrades the NF-κB repressor KLF2 in a feedforward loop downstream of TLR signaling, and its loss in hematopoietic cells increases susceptibility to bacterial infection [PMID:26776519].

RAD23B is a multifunctional scaffold protein that operates at the intersection of nucleotide excision repair (NER) and ubiquitin-proteasome-mediated protein degradation. As the obligate partner of XPC in the XPC–RAD23B heterodimer, RAD23B stimulates global genome NER by enabling one-dimensional diffusion along DNA via hopping, high-affinity recognition of thermodynamically destabilized DNA duplexes rather than chemical lesions per se, DNA bending at damage sites, and recruitment of TFIIH for damage verification [PMID:8756644, PMID:30174301, PMID:31372632, PMID:10734143]. Through its N-terminal UbL domain, RAD23B docks on proteasomal subunit S5a/Rpn10, while its UBA domains bind polyubiquitin chains and can inhibit chain assembly, thereby shuttling ubiquitinated substrates to the proteasome; RAD23B stability itself is regulated by the deubiquitinase PSMD7 and its protein levels are modulated by HDAC6 in a deacetylase-independent manner [PMID:12832454, PMID:14585839, PMID:34512150, PMID:23703321]. PARP1-mediated poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation of RAD23B competes with DNA binding, providing a regulatory switch coupling PARylation signaling to NER initiation, and sequestration of RAD23B into polyglutamine-expanded protein aggregates via its UBA domains destabilizes XPC, linking RAD23B loss-of-function to neurodegenerative pathology [PMID:26170451, PMID:29401586].

SMG8 is a regulatory subunit of the SMG1 kinase complex that modulates nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) by controlling SMG1 kinase activity and mRNA surveillance complex remodeling. SMG8 forms a G-domain heterodimer with SMG9, is recruited to the HEAT repeat arm of SMG1 via SMG9, and possesses a C-terminal kinase inhibitory domain (KID) that occludes the SMG1 catalytic pocket and stabilizes an autoinhibited conformation of the SMG1 insertion domain, thereby suppressing UPF1 phosphorylation [PMID:19417104, PMID:31729466, PMID:34698635]. SMG8 additionally recruits the SMG1 complex to the SURF mRNA surveillance complex and regulates its remodeling into the decay-inducing DECID complex [PMID:19417104]. Complete loss of SMG8 in human cells causes only modest NMD impairment, but renders cells hypersensitive to partial SMG1 inhibition, establishing SMG8 as a nonessential modulator that safeguards NMD robustness; homozygous loss-of-function SMG8 variants in humans lead to increased UPF1 phosphorylation and upregulation of NMD substrate mRNAs, linking SMG8 deficiency to a developmental disorder [PMID:41830328, PMID:33242396].

SRSF6 (SRp55) is a serine/arginine-rich splicing factor that functions as a master regulator of alternative splicing across diverse tissue contexts, with broad roles in cell proliferation, apoptosis, stress responses, and innate immunity. It binds purine-rich exonic splicing enhancers — preferring GAA-triplet motifs — via its two RRM domains (with RRM2 playing a key role), cooperatively engaging RNA with nanomolar affinity to promote or repress exon inclusion depending on binding position relative to the target exon [PMID:9436904, PMID:33376132, PMID:29114070]. Its activity is controlled at multiple levels: phosphorylation by DYRK1A, SRPK1, and Clk/Sty modulates RNA binding and subnuclear localization, Clk/Sty-mediated hyperphosphorylation targets it for proteasomal degradation, USP10 prevents its K48-linked polyubiquitination at K16, and its own mRNA levels are auto-regulated by an SRSF4-promoted poison cassette exon mechanism that couples SRSF6 abundance to hypoxia and stress responses [PMID:22767602, PMID:12549978, PMID:41808072, PMID:36620874]. SRSF6 is frequently amplified or overexpressed in cancers where it reprograms splicing of targets including ZO-1, tenascin-C, BAX, Bim, Fas, HIRA, PICALM, and TPM1 to drive proliferation, EMT, chemoresistance, and metastasis, while in macrophages it controls BAX alternative splicing to regulate mitochondrial DNA-triggered cGAS–interferon signaling and programmed cell death [PMID:23132731, PMID:29114070, PMID:36409059, PMID:39356765].

USP7 is a cysteine deubiquitinase that functions as a master regulator of protein stability across the p53-MDM2 axis, DNA damage response, chromatin regulation, and multiple developmental and oncogenic signaling pathways. Its catalytic domain is intrinsically autoinhibited and requires activation by its C-terminal ubiquitin-like domains (HUBL-45), with further allosteric hyperactivation by GMPS; substrates are recruited primarily through a P/A/ExxS motif that binds the N-terminal TRAF-like domain, which is also exploited by viral proteins such as EBNA1 and KSHV vIRF4 [PMID:16474402, PMID:21981925, PMID:22056774]. USP7 deubiquitinates and stabilizes p53 directly, yet preferentially stabilizes MDM2 and MDMX under basal conditions, establishing a dynamic feedback loop in which CK2 phosphorylation maintains USP7 stability and DNA damage triggers ATM/PPM1G-mediated dephosphorylation to shift the balance toward p53 activation [PMID:11923872, PMID:15053880, PMID:15916963, PMID:22361354]. Beyond p53 signaling, USP7 deubiquitinates substrates spanning chromatin regulation (EZH2, H2BK120ub1, RNF168, KDM5B), DNA repair and replication (Chk1, Rad18, MCM-BP, RRM2), and key signaling effectors (PTEN, FOXO4, HIF-1α, β-catenin, KRAS, YAP/TAZ, Gli, NOTCH1, Raf-1), thereby influencing cell cycle progression, the Hedgehog and Hippo pathways, Wnt signaling, and immune checkpoint regulation [PMID:18716620, PMID:25894431, PMID:25961918, PMID:33849069, PMID:30679505, PMID:39499616, PMID:26120032, PMID:27934968]. USP7 knockout is embryonic lethal in mice, partially rescued by p53 deletion, confirming both p53-dependent and p53-independent essential functions in vivo [PMID:19946331, PMID:21350561].

XRN1 is a conserved, abundant cytoplasmic 5'→3' processive exoribonuclease that serves as the principal engine of cytoplasmic mRNA turnover and coordinates mRNA decay with transcription, translation, and innate immune homeostasis. Crystal and cryo-EM structures show that XRN1 specifically recognizes 5'-monophosphorylated RNA through a basic pocket, channels mRNA from the ribosomal exit site into its active center for co-translational degradation, and is stalled by structured RNA elements such as flaviviral pseudoknots to generate subgenomic flaviviral RNAs [PMID:21362555, PMID:30911188, PMID:24692447]. XRN1 physically couples to the decapping machinery (DCP1/EDC4, Pat1) and the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex through its C-terminal low-complexity region, thereby integrating deadenylation, decapping, and 5'→3' decay into a coordinated pathway; it also functions as a NAD-cap decapping enzyme and participates in rapid tRNA decay [PMID:27078363, PMID:31340047, PMID:35173156, PMID:18443146]. Loss of XRN1 causes accumulation of endogenous double-stranded RNA and activation of the PKR/OAS innate immune sensing pathways, deregulates autophagy through stabilization of ATG transcripts, and disrupts the transcription–decay feedback circuit that buffers mRNA levels [PMID:38261514, PMID:25766294, PMID:29465287, PMID:24119399].

ZFP36L2 is a CCCH tandem zinc finger RNA-binding protein that promotes mRNA decay by recognizing AU-rich elements (preferentially 7-mer UAUUUAU motifs in accessible hairpin loop structures) in target mRNA 3′ UTRs and recruiting the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, a process inhibited by RSK/ERK-mediated phosphorylation that dissociates CCR4-NOT [PMID:14981510, PMID:25106868, PMID:28455422, PMID:38829516]. Through post-transcriptional destabilization of cell cycle regulators (cyclins D1, B1; CDK1; E2F1), signaling intermediates (Mdm2, Notch1, Ikzf2), and differentiation-associated transcripts, ZFP36L2 enforces quiescence and developmental checkpoints in diverse lineages including oocytes, hematopoietic stem cells, erythroid progenitors, thymocytes, and B lymphocytes [PMID:15342461, PMID:19633199, PMID:23748442, PMID:20622884, PMID:27102483]. ZFP36L2 also functions in innate antiviral defense by binding flavivirus RNA and directing its degradation through the XRN1 5′→3′ exonuclease pathway, and by blocking HIV-1 Rev-dependent nuclear export of viral transcripts [PMID:39972499, PMID:41932956]. Pathogenic ZFP36L2 variants cause recurrent preimplantation embryonic arrest in women by disrupting maternal mRNA clearance and the consequent histone methylation program required for oocyte developmental competence [PMID:34611029, PMID:29408237, PMID:39178021].

ZFP91 is a bifunctional zinc-finger protein that operates both as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase and as a transcription factor, linking ubiquitin-dependent proteostasis to transcriptional regulation in immune cells, hematopoietic malignancies, and metabolic reprogramming. As an E3 ligase, ZFP91 ubiquitinates diverse substrates — mediating K48-linked degradation of hnRNP A1 (shifting PKM splicing to suppress the Warburg effect), hnRNP F, FOXA1, E2F2, and TSPYL2, while catalyzing K63-linked ubiquitination of pro-IL-1β to activate caspase-8 inflammasome signaling and ubiquitinating BECN1 to promote autophagosome maturation in regulatory T cells [PMID:32754263, PMID:29706618, PMID:34825365, PMID:33355624, PMID:36375317]. As a transcription factor, ZFP91 directly binds the HIF-1α and EVI1 promoters to activate transcription, enhances activating histone marks (H3K4me3/H3K27ac), and coregulates cell-survival gene programs with IKZF1 in T-cell lymphomas [PMID:27144516, PMID:42034869, PMID:34936696]. ZFP91 is itself an IMiD-dependent neosubstrate of CRL4-CRBN, where lenalidomide and related compounds induce its ubiquitination and degradation through a conserved zinc-finger degron motif [PMID:28530236].

ZMIZ1 is a PIAS-family transcriptional coactivator that enhances the activity of diverse transcription factors—including androgen receptor, p53, Smad3/4, NOTCH1, ERα, and GATA4—by binding them through its TPR and Miz domains, and promotes SUMOylation of substrates such as AR and NLRP3 [PMID:14609956, PMID:16777850, PMID:17584785, PMID:26522984, PMID:40650830]. ZMIZ1 functions as a selective NOTCH1 cofactor at specific enhancer elements, driving Myc expression during the DN-to-DP thymocyte transition and in Notch-induced T-ALL, where single-residue TPR mutations abolish the interaction and impair leukemic proliferation [PMID:26522984, PMID:30076146]. In vivo, ZMIZ1 is essential for embryonic vascular development, endothelial angiogenesis, β-cell maturity and insulin secretion, uterine decidualization and fertility downstream of estrogen receptor signaling, and upper-layer cortical neuron differentiation, where it directly regulates neurodevelopmental target genes including EfnB2 [PMID:17967885, PMID:41104017, PMID:36307047, PMID:41321316, PMID:41633496]. Pathogenic ZMIZ1 variants cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome, and lactylation at K843 stabilizes ZMIZ1 protein by antagonizing its SUMOylation and ubiquitination [PMID:30639322, PMID:40670831].

GSE1 is a chromatin-associated scaffolding protein that functions within the HDAC1/CoREST/BHC (LSD1-containing) co-repressor complex to mediate transcriptional silencing and coordinate the DNA damage response. GSE1 anchors the deubiquitinase USP22 to the CoREST complex, enabling H2B-K120 deubiquitination upon DNA damage without affecting the complex's histone deacetylase activity, and cooperates with HDAC1 to repress target genes including the tumor suppressor KLF6 and immune/cytokine-signaling loci [PMID:37878419, PMID:34862459, PMID:38886911]. GSE1 is required for placental development in mice, where its loss causes embryonic lethality due to deficient syncytiotrophoblast-II differentiation in a placenta-autonomous manner [PMID:37019373]. Overexpression of GSE1 in multiple cancer types promotes proliferation, invasion, and therapy resistance through transcriptional repression of tumor suppressors and modulation of apoptotic gene expression [PMID:26828271, PMID:34439112, PMID:33623790].

RSRC2 is an arginine/serine-rich RNA-binding protein that functions at the intersection of pre-mRNA splicing regulation, transcriptional control, and centrosome-associated mRNA localization to maintain mitotic fidelity and suppress tumor progression. RSRC2 directly binds mRNA in human cells [PMID:22658674] and associates with distinct splicing and centrosome biogenesis complexes; its depletion impairs recruitment of the centrosomal scaffold proteins PCNT and CDK5RAP2, disrupting mitotic spindle organization, and the lncRNA C1QTNF1-AS1 directs RSRC2 to centrosomes where it promotes local recruitment of PCNT mRNA [PMID:41841495]. RSRC2 also functions as a transcriptional repressor of SCIN, and this repression underlies its anti-proliferative, anti-migratory, and anti-invasive activity in triple-negative breast cancer cells, as demonstrated by ChIP-seq and rescue experiments [PMID:38201443]. RSRC2 expression is itself regulated by TRA2A-mediated alternative splicing of its exon 4, producing isoform shifts that modulate protein levels and contribute to paclitaxel resistance [PMID:28416606].
